summary: Explores issues in registering internationalized domain names. The large set of allowed characters can cause confusion between similar-looking names, so registries need rules that disallow some combinations. The memo suggests mechanisms for defining such rules across many languages, including methods adapted from Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4290 suggests ways for domain registries to limit confusing internationalized domain names (IDNs), which use characters beyond basic English letters. Registries can define allowed characters and related forms, then choose which names are registered or reserved.

questions: how to prevent domain name spoofing
what is an idn registration bundle
subtitle: A framework for registries to manage confusing character variants in internationalized domain names.

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names can contain many Unicode characters, including characters that look or behave similarly. Unrestricted registrations can create user confusion, fraud and cybersquatting risks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4290 suggests registry-specific character tables and a registration-bundle process that identifies related variant labels, while leaving each registry choices about what to allow, reserve or publish.
tldr.outcome: The RFC offers non-normative practices for registries to consider. It warns that variants reduce some risks but cannot eliminate all confusion or replace local policy choices.

today: RFC 4290 is an Informational document and its IESG Note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard. It presents suggested practices for registries to consider.

sections.title: Why Registration Rules Matter
sections.content:
IDNA allows non-ASCII strings to be represented in DNS names, but the large character repertoire can include visually or otherwise similar forms. A name using the digit one may be confused with one using a lowercase letter l, even in ASCII. Registries may therefore restrict which otherwise-valid combinations they accept.

RFC 4290 offers a framework for registries to consider; its recommendations are not normative. It adapts ideas from the JET Guidelines for Chinese, Japanese and Korean names, while noting that different languages and scripts may need different rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Some letters or symbols look similar enough that users may mistake one Internet name for another. The RFC suggests that each registry set rules for its users rather than apply one global character list.

sections.title: Base Characters, Variants and Bundles
sections.content:
A base character is one a registry permits in a submitted name. A variant is a character or string that the registry treats as equivalent or similar enough to cause confusion. A registration bundle contains the requested base name and labels produced by expanding its characters into their variants.

A label in a bundle is not automatically registered in DNS. The RFC describes registry choices: activate all labels, reserve all other labels, or activate and reserve selected labels. The registry's policy determines which option applies.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry can group a requested name with related forms. The group does not mean every name is published in the Domain Name System (DNS); the registry chooses which names are active and which are only reserved.

sections.title: Language Tables and Registry Policy
sections.content:
A language table lists the base characters a registry accepts and may list variants for each character. The RFC discusses using separate tables for different languages or scripts and warns that those categories do not map cleanly to every writing system. A registry may also need rules for character sequences, not just individual characters.

Tables use Unicode code points and may be machine-readable. The RFC describes a format in which a base character can be followed by a vertical bar and variant entries. It emphasizes that the format and variant choices are examples for registry policies, not universal rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry publishes a list of characters it accepts and may list related forms. Different registries can make different choices because languages and writing systems do not share one set of rules.

sections.title: How CreateBundle Processes a Name
sections.content:
CreateBundle takes a proposed base name, its language or script designation, and the associated table. First, it rejects the request if any character is not a listed base character. It then applies IDNA's ToASCII operation to the base name; if that fails, registration stops.

If the base name passes, the procedure builds combinations using each character and its listed variants, applies ToASCII to each candidate, and adds successful labels to the bundle. The base registration is included. A table without variants uses the simpler checks of allowed characters and ToASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry first checks that every character is allowed and converts the requested name to the ASCII form used by DNS. It then checks combinations made from listed variants and adds valid names to the group.

sections.title: Benefits and Limits of Variant Rules
sections.content:
Variant rules can bind potentially confusing names to one registrant or prevent separate parties from registering them. They can reduce some opportunities for confusion and fraud, but the RFC says no plausible set of restrictions can eliminate every problem. For example, digit one and lowercase l may be confused in some fonts.

Character-by-character variants do not address every source of confusion, such as a language commonly written in multiple scripts or transliteration across scripts. Registries should balance restrictions against the value of flexible identifiers and consider their language and user communities.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules for similar-looking characters can prevent some confusing names from being registered by different parties. They cannot remove every source of confusion, so each registry must choose rules suited to its users.
